points_of_disagreement: Whether Iran's proposal represents a capitulation by the US or a success for Trump's 'Peace Through Strength' strategy
Whether the proposal adequately addresses Iran's nuclear enrichment program (60% uranium) or leaves the core strategic threat unresolved
Whether Iran's assertion of control over the Strait of Hormuz constitutes a legitimate reconstruction mechanism or a threat to global energy security
Whether the ceasefire process was authorized under existing war powers or violated the War Powers Act
Whether Iran's claim of 'victory' or the US claim of favorable terms is accurate given the same agreement
Whether the humanitarian cost (civilian deaths, displacement, infrastructure damage) invalidates the diplomatic achievement
Whether the absence of a mutually agreed public text indicates a binding agreement or diplomatic theater
Whether the Iranian regime's survival and opposition activists' abandonment represents a strategic failure or acceptable outcome
Whether Pakistan's mediation and China's role strengthen or undermine the legitimacy of any resulting agreement
shared_foundation.summary: All framings accept that Iran submitted a ceasefire proposal containing points on US troop withdrawal, regional conflict cessation, and war reparations, mediated through Pakistan with regional support, and that Iran has enriched uranium to 60% purity. The disagreements center on whether this proposal represents Iranian victory or US success, whether it adequately resolves nuclear proliferation, what its implications are for global energy markets and US war powers law, and whether the humanitarian costs and diplomatic process legitimacy undermine or validate the agreement.

framings.name: Iran's Victory / US Capitulation
framings.question: Did Iran force the United States into an unfavorable settlement that rewards aggression?
framings.key_claim: Iran's 10-to-14-point proposal — demanding US troop withdrawal, war reparations, sanctions relief, and Hormuz control — represents a major capitulation by Washington after a war it launched but could not finish on its own terms.
framings.description: This framing reads Iran's proposal as evidence that the US failed to achieve its stated war aims and is now negotiating from a position of weakness. Iran is portrayed as dictating terms to a superpower that attacked it.
framings.emphasizes: Iran's maximalist demands (troop withdrawal, reparations, enrichment rights, Hormuz sovereignty); Iran's own 'victory' declarations; the gap between pre-war US objectives and the emerging deal.
framings.downplays: The severe damage Iran sustained; its own economic desperation; the genuine military gains the US and Israel made against Iranian infrastructure and leadership.
framings.tone: alarmed | accusatory (from hawks); celebratory (from Iran state media)
sample_headlines: Iran claimed victory, asserting that it had forced the US to accept its 10-point plan (Wikipedia / Reuters)
Iran's 10-Point Peace Plan for Trump: Dissected — 'From the perspective of Iran hawks in Washington, it looks like capitulation' (Newsweek)
What is in Iran's 10-point plan to end the US-Israeli war? (Middle East Eye)

carriers.name: Iran Supreme National Security Council (via state media)
carriers.excerpt: saying it had forced the US to accept its 10-point plan as a basis for talks and described the ceasefire as an 'enduring defeat' for Washington
carriers.role_evidence: Iran's top security body was the first to frame the ceasefire publicly as a US defeat and Iranian victory.

carriers.name: Middle East Eye
carriers.excerpt: it would mark a major capitulation from the US, which attacked Iran alongside Israel at the end of February
carriers.role_evidence: Among the first Western outlets to explicitly use the word 'capitulation' to describe the US posture toward Iran's proposal.

carriers.name: Newsweek
carriers.excerpt: From the perspective of Iran hawks in Washington, it looks like capitulation, giving major financial relief in exchange for promises they do not trust.
carriers.role_evidence: Widely-read dissection of Iran's plan that crystallised the 'capitulation' framing for a broad US audience.

carriers.name: Sen. Roger Wicker (R-MS) / Senate Armed Services Committee
carriers.excerpt: questioned the merit of a proposed 60-day ceasefire, saying it would be a 'disaster.' 'Everything accomplished by Operation Epic Fury would be for naught!'
carriers.role_evidence: Senate Armed Services chair gave the 'capitulation' framing institutional weight by publicly opposing any ceasefire deal from within the GOP.

carriers.name: WION News
carriers.excerpt: Tehran's 10-point plan lays out big demands, from sanctions relief and enrichment rights to control over the Strait of Hormuz and US troop withdrawal.
carriers.role_evidence: Widely circulated explainer that mapped Iran's maximalist demands in full, amplifying the 'Iran is winning' framing to a global English-language audience.

framings.name: Peace Through Strength / Trump Deal-Making
framings.question: Is the Trump administration successfully leveraging military and economic pressure to force Iran into a comprehensive and unprecedented deal?
framings.key_claim: US military dominance and a naval blockade have brought Iran to the negotiating table on terms far more ambitious than Obama-era diplomacy, and Trump's 'Peace Through Strength' approach is producing tangible progress toward ending decades of Iranian threats.
framings.description: This framing presents Iran's proposal not as a US defeat but as proof that coercive pressure worked. Iran's willingness to negotiate at all — and to reopen the Strait — is cast as a win for Trump's confrontational approach.
framings.emphasizes: Iran agreeing to open the Strait; Trump's description of the 10-point plan as a 'workable basis'; the contrast with the failed Obama JCPOA; US military successes in Operation Epic Fury.
framings.downplays: Iran's maximalist demands that remain unmet; ongoing ceasefire violations; the $29B+ military cost; congressional resistance; Iran's continued near-weapons-grade uranium stockpile.
sample_headlines: Trump: Iranian 10-point proposal is 'workable basis on which to negotiate' (Truth Social / AFP)
One Senator applauded President Trump's 'Peace Through Strength leadership' (CRS/Congress.gov)
Trump says deal with Iran including opening Strait of Hormuz is 'largely negotiated' (AP/PBS)

carriers.name: Donald Trump / Truth Social
carriers.excerpt: Almost all of the various points of past contention have been agreed to between the United States and Iran
carriers.role_evidence: Trump himself coined and distributed the 'workable basis' framing of Iran's proposal directly via Truth Social.

carriers.name: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA)
carriers.excerpt: 'Remember … Iran declared war on us 47 years ago.'
carriers.role_evidence: Johnson publicly defended the war and opposed the War Powers resolution, providing institutional GOP backing for the 'strength works' narrative.

carriers.name: White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller
carriers.excerpt: claimed Iranian regime has made significant concessions in the negotiations like reopening the strait
carriers.role_evidence: Miller amplified the 'concessions are being won' framing from inside the White House communications apparatus.

carriers.name: Secretary of State Marco Rubio
carriers.excerpt: negotiations were addressing both Iran's enrichment capabilities as well as its enriched material
carriers.role_evidence: Rubio publicly framed ongoing talks as substantively addressing US red lines, bolstering the 'deal is being won' narrative.

framings.name: Nuclear Non-Proliferation Imperative
framings.question: Does Iran's proposal adequately resolve the nuclear threat that was the stated justification for the war?
framings.key_claim: Iran's ceasefire proposal leaves the core nuclear question unanswered — its near-weapons-grade uranium stockpile and enrichment program survive — meaning any deal that doesn't address this fails the original strategic test.
framings.description: This framing, dominant among national security analysts and bipartisan foreign policy institutions, evaluates Iran's proposal primarily through the lens of nuclear nonproliferation. It asks whether the ceasefire will reduce or lock in Iran's nuclear breakout capability.
framings.emphasizes: Iran's ~440kg of uranium enriched to 60%; Iran's inclusion of 'acceptance of enrichment' in some versions of the plan; the US demand for full dismantlement; the gap between the two sides on this single issue.
framings.downplays: Human costs of continuing the war; economic disruption from the Strait closure; the feasibility of Iran agreeing to full dismantlement.
sample_headlines: Iran's nuclear program has been at the center of the U.S.-Iran conflict for decades (CSIS)
Trump: 'The most important thing is nuclear, and that was not agreed to' (PBS/AP)
Any agreement 'relating to the nuclear program of Iran' would trigger congressional review (CRS)

carriers.name: CSIS (Center for Strategic and International Studies) / Daniel Byman
carriers.excerpt: The nuclear issue is unresolved, Lebanon is destabilized, the risk of terrorism persists, and U.S. alliances have been strained
carriers.role_evidence: CSIS published the most widely-cited early analysis foregrounding nuclear non-resolution as the ceasefire's central flaw.

carriers.name: Congressional Research Service (CRS)
carriers.excerpt: Any agreement 'relating to the nuclear program of Iran' would trigger congressional review requirements under the 2015 Iran Nuclear Agreement Review Act
carriers.role_evidence: CRS formally institutionalised the nuclear framing for Congress, making it the default analytical lens for members reviewing the deal.

carriers.name: Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu
carriers.excerpt: the most important objective is the removal of all enriched material from Iran and the dismantling of Iran's enrichment capabilities
carriers.role_evidence: Netanyahu's red-line statements gave the nuclear-first framing powerful international amplification and complicated US-Iran talks.

carriers.name: Al Jazeera English
carriers.excerpt: Some analysts say Iran may have to change its tone on its nuclear programme.
carriers.role_evidence: Al Jazeera's ongoing ceasefire coverage systematically flagged the nuclear gap as the pivotal obstacle, reaching a global mass audience.

carriers.name: Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth
carriers.excerpt: we stand ready in the background to ensure that Iran upholds the terms of the ceasefire agreement
carriers.role_evidence: Hegseth's warnings kept the military-enforcement dimension of the nuclear framing alive in official US communications.

framings.name: Human Cost / Civilian Harm
framings.question: Who has been hurt, and does any proposed deal adequately account for the civilians killed, displaced, and impoverished by the war?
framings.key_claim: The ceasefire proposal arrives after thousands of Iranian and Lebanese civilians — including children at schools and patients in hospitals — have already been killed or displaced, and a paper agreement cannot undo the humanitarian catastrophe already underway.
framings.description: This framing foregrounds the lived experience of civilians across Iran, Lebanon, Iraq, and the Gulf. It evaluates Iran's demand for war reparations and compensation through the lens of documented civilian harm rather than geopolitical bargaining.
framings.emphasizes: Documented civilian death tolls (3,600+ in Iran; 1,700+ in Lebanon); destruction of hospitals, schools, and water infrastructure; the reparations clause in Iran's proposal as acknowledgment of harm; environmental contamination.
framings.downplays: Iran's strategic use of civilian harm claims for diplomatic leverage; the regime's own violence against protesters prior to the war; military objectives that justified some strikes.
sample_headlines: Almost 4,000 Iranians have been killed by U.S.-Israeli strikes, including at least 175 students at a girls' elementary school (FCNL)
The Human and Environmental Costs of the War in Iran (Center for American Progress)
The humanitarian consequences of the US-Israeli war on Iran should not be understood as isolated incidents (Arab Center DC)

carriers.name: Arab Center Washington DC / Yara M. Asi
carriers.excerpt: Since the war started, we have seen children killed in their classrooms, hospitals rendered inoperable, millions displaced from their homes
carriers.role_evidence: Among the first think-tank publications to systematically document and frame civilian harm as the primary lens for evaluating the ceasefire.

carriers.name: Center for American Progress
carriers.excerpt: strikes have expanded into civilian and industrial infrastructure… harms that fall on communities already living at the margins of environmental tolerance
carriers.role_evidence: CAP's detailed report extended the humanitarian framing to include environmental/radiological risks, broadening the harm narrative.

carriers.name: Friends Committee on National Legislation (FCNL)
carriers.excerpt: Almost 4,000 Iranians have been killed by U.S.-Israeli strikes, including at least 175 people, mostly young students
carriers.role_evidence: FCNL directly lobbied Congress using civilian casualty statistics, translating the humanitarian framing into legislative pressure.

carriers.name: Human Rights Watch / Sarah Yager
carriers.excerpt: targeting Iranian infrastructure, including power plants, would violate international law if it causes harm to civilians that is excessive
carriers.role_evidence: HRW's legal framing of civilian harm provided the authoritative rights-based anchor for the broader humanitarian narrative.

carriers.name: Wikipedia / Casualties of the 2026 Iran War (aggregating HRANA, Red Crescent, UN data)
carriers.excerpt: HRANA documented 3,636 deaths in Iran due to strikes, including 1,701 civilians
carriers.role_evidence: Widely linked Wikipedia casualty page served as an ongoing reference amplifying documented civilian death statistics across social media.

framings.name: War Powers / Constitutional Accountability
framings.question: Did the executive branch conduct an unauthorized war, and does any peace deal require congressional consent?
framings.key_claim: The Trump administration launched and sustained a major war without congressional authorization, then attempted to declare the war 'terminated' via ceasefire to avoid the 60-day War Powers Act deadline — and now any Iran deal involving nuclear terms requires mandatory congressional review.
framings.description: This framing, championed by legal scholars, bipartisan members of Congress, and civil liberties groups, centers on the constitutional and statutory constraints on executive war-making. It scrutinizes the ceasefire proposal primarily as a legal and legislative question.
framings.emphasizes: The 60-day War Powers Act deadline; the House passing a war powers resolution 215-208; Trump's claim the war was 'terminated'; the 2015 Iran Nuclear Agreement Review Act's trigger provisions; the $29B war cost without supplemental appropriations.
framings.downplays: The strategic rationale for fast executive action; the difficulty of legislating during active hostilities; whether a slower congressional process could have achieved better outcomes.
sample_headlines: House passes war powers resolution directing Trump to end hostilities with Iran (NPR)
Trump rejects Iran's latest proposal as he reviews new military options — White House claims war 'terminated' to avoid War Powers deadline (PBS NewsHour)
Some Members have indicated intention to introduce measures under the War Powers Resolution 'to end this conflict permanently' (CRS)

carriers.name: PBS NewsHour / Nick Schifrin
carriers.excerpt: the White House informed Congress it didn't need to get its approval because the war had been 'terminated' during the current cease-fire
carriers.role_evidence: PBS was among the first to broadcast the White House's contested legal claim and immediately juxtaposed it with expert critique, originating the 'pause button' legal debate.

carriers.name: Prof. Harold Koh, Yale Law School
carriers.excerpt: It's as if the president is trying to rewrite the war powers resolution and add a pause button
carriers.role_evidence: Koh's quote on PBS crystallised legal opposition to the White House's war-powers interpretation and was widely cited afterward.

carriers.name: NPR / Mariam Zuhaib
carriers.excerpt: A bipartisan majority in the Republican-led House voted on Wednesday to end the war with Iran, the clearest rebuke yet of President Trump's handling of the conflict
carriers.role_evidence: NPR's House vote reporting brought the war powers framing to a massive public radio audience at the moment of maximum legislative impact.

carriers.name: Congressional Research Service (CRS)
carriers.excerpt: Any agreement 'relating to the nuclear program of Iran' would trigger congressional review requirements under the 2015 Iran Nuclear Agreement Review Act
carriers.role_evidence: CRS formally embedded the war-powers and INARA review requirements into official congressional deliberations.

carriers.name: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) / Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-PA)
carriers.excerpt: Fitzpatrick told reporters he chose to support the resolution because 'we have to follow the law,' referring to the War Powers Act
carriers.role_evidence: Republican defectors gave the war-powers framing bipartisan legitimacy and became the story's dominant news hook.

framings.name: Global Economic Disruption / Energy Security
framings.question: What are the global economic consequences of the Strait of Hormuz closure and how does Iran's proposal affect energy markets and inflation?
framings.key_claim: Iran's proposal to assert a 'new mechanism' over the Strait of Hormuz — including transit fees and de facto Iranian control — threatens to permanently restructure global energy flows and embed new inflationary pressures into the world economy regardless of whether fighting stops.
framings.description: This framing is dominant in business and financial press, treating the ceasefire proposal primarily as an economic and commodity-markets event. The Strait of Hormuz provision in Iran's plan is read as an attempt to monetize a critical global chokepoint.
framings.emphasizes: Strait of Hormuz carrying 20% of global oil/LNG; Iran and Oman's transit fee scheme for reconstruction; rising oil prices; US blockade's impact on Iranian oil exports; inflation effects on US consumers.
framings.downplays: Humanitarian civilian harm; the nuclear security dimension; the broader regional political stakes.
sample_headlines: The rising price of oil and lack of a deal to open the Strait of Hormuz are denting stocks and driving up inflation (US News)
Iran and Oman plan to charge transit fees for vessels passing through the strait, with funds earmarked for reconstruction (CNN/Tasnim)
The conflict has disrupted regional energy production and maritime and air transit with global economic impacts (CRS)

carriers.name: CNN / International Desk
carriers.excerpt: Iran and Oman plan to charge transit fees for vessels passing through the strait during the ceasefire, with the funds earmarked for reconstruction
carriers.role_evidence: CNN was among the first English-language outlets to report the transit-fee mechanism, making it a core part of global economic coverage.

carriers.name: US News & World Report
carriers.excerpt: The rising price of oil and lack of a deal to open the Strait of Hormuz are denting stocks and driving up inflation.
carriers.role_evidence: US News framed Iran's latest proposal explicitly through consumer inflation and stock market impact, reaching a broad financial-news audience.

carriers.name: Friends Committee on National Legislation (FCNL)
carriers.excerpt: Prior to the war, roughly 20 percent of the world's oil and liquid natural gas shipments transited through the strait.
carriers.role_evidence: FCNL linked the Hormuz economic disruption to its anti-militarism argument, spreading the energy-security framing into progressive advocacy circles.

carriers.name: Gulf Business / Regional Business Press
carriers.excerpt: Trump issued an ultimatum regarding the Strait of Hormuz, threatening military action before agreeing to a two-week ceasefire contingent on its opening.
carriers.role_evidence: Gulf Business provided regional private-sector perspectives on Hormuz disruption, amplifying the economic framing to Middle East and Asia Pacific business audiences.

framings.name: Diplomatic Process / Mediator Legitimacy
framings.question: Is the US-Iran negotiating framework — mediated by Pakistan, involving China and Oman — a credible and durable diplomatic architecture, or a fragile back-channel that neither side intends to honor?
framings.key_claim: The ceasefire proposal process, conducted through Pakistani intermediaries with China, Oman, and Turkey playing supporting roles, exposes both the absence of direct US-Iran diplomatic relations and the difficulty of binding agreements when the two sides publicly describe incompatible deals.
framings.description: This framing, common among foreign policy analysts, diplomacy correspondents, and regional governments, evaluates the procedural legitimacy and structural fragility of the ceasefire architecture itself — not just what the deal says, but whether the process can produce enforceable terms.
framings.emphasizes: Pakistan's mediation role; the lack of any publicly released mutual text; Iran producing multiple incompatible versions of its 10-point plan; both sides claiming victory from the same agreement; China's supportive role.
framings.downplays: The substantive content of the proposals; domestic political pressures on each side; the nuclear question.
sample_headlines: No text reflecting mutual agreement on ceasefire terms was released, and the two sides' differing public statements presaged subsequent points of tension (CRS)
A Pakistani source says US, Iran 'keep changing their goalposts' (Times of Israel)
Iran has reportedly produced at least two versions of a 10-point proposal that may differ from each other (CRS / EveryCRSReport)

carriers.name: Congressional Research Service (CRS)
carriers.excerpt: Iran has reportedly produced at least two versions of a 10-point proposal that may differ from each other, as well as from the version referenced by President Trump.
carriers.role_evidence: CRS first formally documented the 'two incompatible texts' problem, originating the process-legitimacy framing for congressional audiences.

carriers.name: Times of Israel
carriers.excerpt: Pakistani source says US, Iran 'keep changing their goalposts'
carriers.role_evidence: Times of Israel sourced a Pakistani mediator's candid frustration, giving the 'broken process' framing a concrete named-country source.

carriers.name: Al Jazeera / Resul Serdar Atas (Tehran correspondent)
carriers.excerpt: both sides are still interested in diplomatically engaging with each other… Iranian officials are saying that several US demands are unreasonable, unrealistic and maximalist
carriers.role_evidence: Al Jazeera's Tehran-based reporting gave the 'deeply divergent frameworks' framing global reach via continuous ceasefire coverage.

carriers.name: Financial Times
carriers.excerpt: the US pushed Pakistan to broker a temporary ceasefire in early April
carriers.role_evidence: FT reporting on US pressure on Pakistan to broker the deal revealed the behind-the-scenes fragility of the mediation architecture.

carriers.name: Prof. Paul Musgrave, Georgetown University
carriers.excerpt: Trump seems to have rejected the new Iranian proposal 'without reading it or being briefed on it'
carriers.role_evidence: Musgrave's academic critique of Trump's ad-hoc rejection challenged the administration's framing that it was conducting serious process-driven diplomacy.

framings.name: Iranian Regime Survival / Domestic Resilience
framings.question: Has the war and the ceasefire proposal strengthened or weakened the Islamic Republic's grip on power, and what does this mean for Iranians who want regime change?
framings.key_claim: Despite losing its supreme leader and suffering massive military damage, the Islamic Republic has survived the onslaught, used the ceasefire to claim a moral victory, and left Iranian opposition and pro-democracy activists feeling abandoned by both their own government and the United States.
framings.description: This framing, dominant in Iranian diaspora media and human rights advocacy, scrutinizes the ceasefire proposal as an implicit US endorsement of the Islamic Republic's continued rule. It highlights the regime's resilience and the frustration of Iranians who hoped for liberation.
framings.emphasizes: Iran's claim of a 'great victory'; the absence of regime change among final US objectives; the brutal January 2026 crackdown that preceded the war; the Iranian opposition's mixed reaction to the ceasefire.
framings.downplays: The genuine military degradation Iran suffered; the political realism of regime-change goals; Iran's civilian population's stated desire for peace.
sample_headlines: The Islamic Republic's clerical leadership withstood the superpower onslaught with no sign of organized opposition (Times of Israel)
Iran International: ceasefire drew mixed reactions from opposition — some felt Trump abandoned them (Wikipedia/Iran International)
Trump and Netanyahu said they launched the war to create conditions for Iranians to topple their rulers — but the war has yet to achieve that (US News)

carriers.name: Iran International
carriers.excerpt: some expressing outrage and despair, feeling that Trump abandoned them and left the country in a worse state than it was before the war began
carriers.role_evidence: Iran International, the leading diaspora Persian-language outlet, was the first to systematically report and frame opposition reaction to the ceasefire as betrayal.

carriers.name: Times of Israel
carriers.excerpt: The Islamic Republic's clerical leadership, which had faced a mass uprising at the start of the year, withstood the superpower onslaught with no sign of organized opposition.
carriers.role_evidence: Times of Israel repeatedly foregrounded regime survival as the key metric for evaluating the ceasefire outcome, amplifying the framing to pro-Israel and hawkish audiences.

carriers.name: US News & World Report
carriers.excerpt: Trump and Netanyahu said they launched the war to curb Iran's support for regional militias… but the war has yet to deprive Iran of its stockpile of near-weapons-grade enriched uranium
carriers.role_evidence: US News framed the ceasefire proposal against Trump's original stated war objectives, giving the 'regime survived' narrative wide American readership.

carriers.name: Center for American Progress
carriers.excerpt: Between late December 2025 and late January 2026, anti-government protests spread to more than 200 cities across Iran… the ensuing crackdown resulted in massacres that left thousands of protesters dead
carriers.role_evidence: CAP highlighted the pre-war crackdown context, embedding the 'regime survived and was legitimised' narrative within a human rights framework.

gap_analysis: Missing are framings centered on: (1) Gulf state allies' security concerns and their potential exclusion from negotiations despite direct regional stakes; (2) the practical implementation/verification mechanics of proposed terms—how would troop withdrawal, damage assessment, or conflict cessation actually be monitored or enforced; (3) domestic Iranian political economy perspectives—how ceasefire terms affect different factions within Iran's government or public; (4) historical precedent analysis—how this proposal compares structurally to past failed/successful regional agreements; and (5) non-state actor implications—how proxy forces, militias, or non-governmental armed groups would be addressed or constrained by such terms.
